collins.hedgehog: Run the bank like a business, with relentless cost discipline, focused on the western United States where it could be the best, rather than trying to be a global bank. Economic denominator: profit per employee.
hedgehog_key_points: run the bank like a business / cost discipline
focus on the western U.S. (not a global bank)
collins.stop_doing: Exit most international banking and close the European offices, and cut costs hard: about 100 branches and 3,000 jobs eliminated, executive perks and frills cut, executive pay held down, starting at the top.
stop_doing_key_points: exit international banking / close overseas offices
cut branches, staff and executive perks
stop trying to be everything a big bank does
collins.leader_type: Level 5 (Carl Reichardt: plain-spoken, frugal, low-profile; built on the strong team that his predecessor Dick Cooley had assembled)
brutal_facts: deregulation will end cheap deposits and turn banking into a more commodity-like business
costs are too high for a deregulated market
it cannot beat the giant money-center banks globally
overseas ventures have repeatedly lost money

later_history: 1983-1998 cumulative stock returns about 3.99x the general market (per Collins). Bought Crocker National (1986, about $1.1B) and Barclays Bank of California (1988); won a hostile bid for First Interstate (1996, $11.3B) with a troubled integration. Acquired by Norwest in 1998, which kept the Wells Fargo name. Bought Wachovia in 2008. In 2016 the fake-accounts scandal broke: sales pressure had led employees to open millions of unauthorized accounts; the bank paid $185M in initial fines and CEO John Stumpf resigned. The Federal Reserve capped its asset growth in 2018; it paid $3B in 2020 to settle criminal and civil probes. The asset cap was lifted in 2025.
notes: Track A matched pair with A22 (Bank of America). Wells Fargo is also a Track B decline candidate at a ~2011 date; keep both in the same dev/held-out split.
